title: I-power torsion modules are unchanged by a flat base change that is an isomorphism modulo I
statement: Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a flat ring map of commutative rings [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map] and $I\subseteq R$ an ideal such that the ring map $R/I\to S/IS$ induced by $\varphi$ is an isomorphism ($IS$ the ideal of $S$ generated by $\varphi(I)$). An $R$-module $T$ is *$I$-power torsion* if for every $x\in T$ there is $n\ge1$ with $I^nx=0$. Then for every $I$-power torsion $R$-module $T$ the $R$-linear map $T\to T\otimes_RS$, $x\mapsto x\otimes1$, to the base change of $T$ [def-weil-module-base-change] is bijective.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E9 (lemma-neighbourhood-isomorphism, line 24264), implication (2) => (1); its standing hypothesis, the equivalent conditions of Lemma 05E7 (lemma-characterize-flatness-on-torsion), holds because an isomorphism R/I -> S/IS is faithfully flat (as used at the start of the proof of Lemma 05EC)

proof.text: *Set-up.* For an $R$-module $M$ write $c_M:M\to M\otimes_RS$, $x\mapsto x\otimes1$, for the $R$-linear map to the base change [def-weil-module-base-change] ($M\otimes_RS$ an $R$-module via $\varphi$). It is natural: for an $R$-linear $u:M\to N$ one has $(u\otimes1)\circ c_M=c_N\circ u$, since $(u\otimes1)(x\otimes1)=u(x)\otimes1$. For $n\ge1$ let $P(n)$ be the claim: *for every $R$-module $M$ with $I^nM=0$ the map $c_M$ is bijective.* Steps 2 and 3 prove $P(n)$ for all $n\ge1$ by induction on $n$ (base $P(1)$, step $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$), and step 4 passes to an arbitrary $I$-power torsion module $T$. Only the flatness of $\varphi$ and the bijectivity of $R/I\to S/IS$ are used; the faithful flatness in the standing hypothesis of Lemma 05E7 is not needed for this implication.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E9 (lemma-neighbourhood-isomorphism, line 24264), proof of (2) => (1), lines 24277-24298

proof.text: *Base case $P(1)$: $M$ annihilated by $I$.* The source writes $M\otimes_RS=M\otimes_{R/I}S/IS=M\otimes_{R/I}R/I=M$; explicitly: let $\psi:R/I\to S/IS$ be the given isomorphism, $\psi(\bar a)=\varphi(a)\bmod IS$, and $\psi^{-1}$ its inverse, a ring isomorphism. Since $IM=0$, $M$ is an $R/I$-module. The map $M\times S\to M$, $(x,s)\mapsto\psi^{-1}(s\bmod IS)\,x$ is $R$-bilinear ($\psi^{-1}(\varphi(a)s\bmod IS)=\bar a\,\psi^{-1}(\bar s)$ as $\psi^{-1}$ is multiplicative and $\psi^{-1}(\overline{\varphi(a)})=\bar a$), so it induces an $R$-linear $r:M\otimes_RS\to M$ with $r(x\otimes s)=\psi^{-1}(\bar s)x$ [def-weil-module-base-change]. Then $r(c_M(x))=\psi^{-1}(\bar1)x=x$. Conversely let $x\in M$, $s\in S$ and choose $a\in R$ with $\psi(\bar a)=\bar s$, i.e. $s=\varphi(a)+\sum_k\varphi(i_k)s_k$ with $i_k\in I$, $s_k\in S$. Then $x\otimes s=x\otimes\varphi(a)+\sum_k x\otimes\varphi(i_k)s_k=ax\otimes1+\sum_k i_kx\otimes s_k=ax\otimes1$ because $i_kx=0$, while $c_M(r(x\otimes s))=\bar a x\otimes1=ax\otimes1$. So $c_M\circ r$ is the identity on the generators $x\otimes s$, hence on $M\otimes_RS$. Thus $c_M$ is bijective with inverse $r$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E9 (lemma-neighbourhood-isomorphism, line 24264), proof of (2) => (1), lines 24277-24298 (first case: M annihilated by I)

proof.text: *Induction step $P(n)\Rightarrow P(n+1)$.* Assume $P(n)$ and let $I^{n+1}M=0$. Put $M'=I^nM$ (the submodule generated by the $ax$, $a\in I^n$, $x\in M$) and $M''=M/I^nM$, with the inclusion $j:M'\to M$ and the projection $p:M\to M''$, so $0\to M'\xrightarrow{j}M\xrightarrow{p}M''\to0$ is exact. Then $IM'\subseteq I^{n+1}M=0$ and $I^nM''=0$ (as $I^nM\subseteq M'$), so $c_{M'}$ is bijective by $P(1)$ (step 2) and $c_{M''}$ by $P(n)$. Since $S$ is a flat $R$-module [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map], tensoring the exact $0\to M'\to M\to M''$ gives the exact $0\to M'\otimes_RS\xrightarrow{j\otimes1}M\otimes_RS\xrightarrow{p\otimes1}M''\otimes_RS$ [lem-weil-pbc-flat-tensor-exact], and $p\otimes1$ is surjective by right exactness of the tensor product applied to $M'\to M\to M''\to0$ [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-right-exact]; so the second row $0\to M'\otimes_RS\to M\otimes_RS\to M''\otimes_RS\to0$ is short exact. By naturality (step 1) $(j\otimes1)\circ c_{M'}=c_M\circ j$ and $(p\otimes1)\circ c_M=c_{M''}\circ p$, so $c_{M'},c_M,c_{M''}$ form a morphism between the two short exact rows in the abelian category of $R$-modules [lem-weil-pbc-ring-modules-enough-injectives], whose isomorphisms are the bijective $R$-linear maps. As $c_{M'}$ and $c_{M''}$ are isomorphisms, so is $c_M$ by the short five lemma [lem-weil-pbc-short-five-lemma]. This proves $P(n+1)$, hence $P(n)$ for every $n\ge1$.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05E9 (lemma-neighbourhood-isomorphism, line 24264), proof of (2) => (1), lines 24277-24298 (induction with 0 -> I^nM -> M -> M/I^nM -> 0)

proof.text: *General $I$-power torsion $T$.* For $n\ge1$ let $T_n=\{x\in T: I^nx=0\}$, a submodule with $I^nT_n=0$, and $T_n\subseteq T_m$ for $n\le m$ (as $I^m\subseteq I^n$); write $\iota_n:T_n\to T$ and $\iota_{nm}:T_n\to T_m$ for the inclusions. (a) $(T,(\iota_n)_n)$ is a colimit of the diagram $n\mapsto T_n$ over the directed set $(\mathbb Z_{\ge1},\le)$ in the category of $R$-modules [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]: it is a cocone; given a cocone $(N,(\mu_n))$, $\mu_m$ restricts to $\mu_n$ on $T_n$, and $T=\bigcup_nT_n$ because $T$ is $I$-power torsion, so $u(x)=\mu_n(x)$ for any $n$ with $x\in T_n$ is a well defined map, $R$-linear (two elements lie in a common $T_n$), with $u\circ\iota_n=\mu_n$, and it is the only such map. (b) By the commutation of tensor products with colimits [lem-weil-pbc-tensor-commutes-with-colimits] (with $N=S$), $(T\otimes_RS,(\iota_n\otimes1)_n)$ is a colimit of $n\mapsto T_n\otimes_RS$ with transition maps $\iota_{nm}\otimes1$. (c) Each $c_{T_n}$ is bijective by step 3, and by naturality (step 1) $(\iota_{nm}\otimes1)\circ c_{T_n}=c_{T_m}\circ\iota_{nm}$ and $(\iota_n\otimes1)\circ c_{T_n}=c_T\circ\iota_n$. (d) The maps $\iota_n\circ c_{T_n}^{-1}:T_n\otimes_RS\to T$ form a cocone on the diagram of (b) ($\iota_m\circ c_{T_m}^{-1}\circ(\iota_{nm}\otimes1)=\iota_m\circ\iota_{nm}\circ c_{T_n}^{-1}=\iota_n\circ c_{T_n}^{-1}$ by (c)), so by (b) there is an $R$-linear $d:T\otimes_RS\to T$ with $d\circ(\iota_n\otimes1)=\iota_n\circ c_{T_n}^{-1}$. Then $d\circ c_T\circ\iota_n=d\circ(\iota_n\otimes1)\circ c_{T_n}=\iota_n$ for all $n$, so $d\circ c_T=\mathrm{id}_T$ by the uniqueness in (a); and $c_T\circ d\circ(\iota_n\otimes1)=c_T\circ\iota_n\circ c_{T_n}^{-1}=\iota_n\otimes1$ for all $n$, so $c_T\circ d=\mathrm{id}$ by the uniqueness in (b). Hence $c_T:T\to T\otimes_RS$, $x\mapsto x\otimes1$, is bijective.
